title: Epaminondas Honors the Lowliest Office
text:
Epaminondas was the Theban general who broke Sparta's military power at Leuctra in 371 BC and became one of the most admired men in Greece. He also had enemies at home in Thebes who resented his influence.

Plutarch, in his essay of advice to politicians known as Precepts of Statecraft, tells how those rivals once tried to humiliate him. Out of envy and as an insult, they had him elected telmarch, a minor city official whose job was to keep the alleys clear of dung and to see that rainwater drained away from the streets. It was a post no one of standing would want.

Epaminondas did not refuse it or treat it with contempt. He took it on and did the work seriously. Plutarch says that he remarked that it is not only the office that shows what kind of man holds it, but also the man who shows what the office is. By the way he carried out the job, he raised the telmarchy, which until then had been nothing but a sort of supervision of street cleaning, to a position of dignity.

Plutarch offers the story to men entering public life, as a model for taking small duties seriously.
lesson: Do the small job you are given as if it mattered. The way you fill a role can raise the role, whatever others meant by giving it to you.
source: Plutarch, Moralia, Precepts of Statecraft (Praecepta gerendae reipublicae), 811b
